guides.title: Sabarimala and the five Ayyappa shrines

intro.html:
Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa

Sabarimala

The Vedic seers looked for the Divine in rivers, seashores and mountain peaks, and Hindu shrines still sit in those places today. A hill shrine asks more of the pilgrim: you have to climb to reach it, and the climb itself becomes part of the worship. No hill shrine is quite like Sabarimala. It stands deep in the forests of the Western Ghats in Keralam and is the abode of Lord Ayyappan.

In the Vedas, Rudra is praised as the lord of all beings and Vishnu as the sustainer of the worlds. Lord Ayyappan is born of both. The Puranas tell how Lord Shiva and Mohini, the enchanting form of Lord Vishnu, came together to bring forth Hariharaputra, the son of Hari and Hara. His name Dharma Shastha comes from the Sanskrit root śās, “to rule and to teach.” It marks him as the one who upholds dharma and guides seekers toward it. Because he is the son of both Shiva and Vishnu, he stands as a living symbol of unity and harmony.

The Bhutanatha Upakhyanam, preserved in the Brahmanda Purana, tells his earthly story. He was raised as Manikantan by King Rajashekhara of Pandalam. When his mission was complete, he chose to dwell at Sabarimala. Before leaving, he revealed to the king that the child he had raised was Maha Shastha himself, and he taught the king the wisdom of the Supreme Self. That teaching is remembered as the Bhutanatha Gita. Bhutanatha means Lord of All Beings. Devotees also call him Harihara Puthran, Ayyanar and Manikantan.

Sabarimala Virtual Q: how to book your darshan slot

blocks.html:
The Bhutanatha Upakhyanam tells how Parashurama raised Keralam from the sea and asked the Lord to protect it. Shastha agreed to stay and told Parashurama to build temples for him, and tradition counts 108 shrines, the Nuttiettu Shasthalayangal. Kulathupuzha is one of the most loved of them.

The temple sits in the forest on the Thiruvananthapuram–Shenkottah road, on the banks of the Kulathupuzha, a tributary of the Kallada River. The Lord is worshipped here as Bala Shastha, the child Veeramanikantan. The story goes that an elderly Brahmin was on his way home from Rameswaram and tried to break a stone to rest his cooking pot on. Blood flowed from the stone, and he realized the Lord was present in it. The Lord is still worshipped in that broken stone, and a Panchaloha vigraha was added later for alankaram. In the tradition of the six Shastha kshetras, Kulathupuzha stands for the Anahata, the heart chakra.

Aryankavu lies 22 km from Shenkottah on the Tamil Nadu border. In ancient times this place was called Arya Vanam, and the temple sits 35 feet below the road. Tradition holds it to be the foremost of the temples Parashurama established. The Lord appears with agni kesham, hair like flames, holding a bunch of flowers, and his Panchaloha murti glows with majesty.

Aryankavu also has a love story. A silk merchant’s daughter from the Sourashtra weaving community of Madurai was devoted to the Lord, and she stayed at the temple while her father traveled to Thiruvananthapuram. On his way back, a wild elephant charged him and a hunter saved his life. The hunter asked for the daughter’s hand, and the father agreed. That night the Lord came to the priests in a dream and asked them to bring the girl dressed as a bride. In the morning she was gone. When the sanctum was opened, the Lord stood there as Kalyana Sundaran, wearing the shawl the merchant had given the hunter, with a small image of Pushkala beside him. The Travancore Devaswom Board still holds the Thrikalyanam every Dhanu month, and the Sourashtra community takes part as the bride’s family. The temple is linked to the Manipura chakra.

Achankovil is deep in the forest. Pilgrims drive through winding roads and villages, and even cross into Tamil Nadu, before they reach it. The Skanda, Padma and Brahmanda Puranas call the Lord Poorna Pushkala Samedhan, and here he appears as Manikanta Muthaiyan with Poorna and Pushkala on either side. They stand for Iccha Shakti and Kriya Shakti, the powers of divine will and divine action. Achankovil is one of the few temples where the original vigraha installed by Parashurama is still worshipped. In ancient times Siddhas worshipped the Lord here with the Vedic Sarpa Suktam, and the temple is still famous for curing snake bites. The temple is linked to the Svadhishthana chakra.

blocks.alt: Entrance to the Erumeli Sree Dharmashastha temple

blocks.html:
Erumeli is about 60 km from Kottayam and was once called Mahishi Marika Vanam. Here the Lord, who loves the forest (poongaavanam), is Kiratha Shastha, the divine hunter, and Petta Shastha. Every year pilgrims dance the Petta Thullal here. Custom asks only Kanni Ayyappans, first-time pilgrims, to dance, but about half of all pilgrims join in.

The main day is 27 Dhanu, around January 10, when the Ambalapuzha and Alangadu yogams lead the dance. The Ambalapuzha group starts only after a Krishna parunthu (kite) circles over the Kochambalam, opposite the mosque of Vavar. Devotees believe the kite is Garuda bringing Sree Krishna of Ambalapuzha to watch. The Alangadu group waits for a bright star to appear at noon. Some say the dance remembers Ayyappan and his companion Vavar preparing their army. Others say people danced for joy when the Lord killed the fierce buffalo demon (eruma), which gave the town its name. Erumeli is linked to the Vishuddha chakra.

Elevation~3,000 ft
Vratam42 days
Main seasonNov – Jan

Sabarimala rises about 3,000 feet in the Western Ghats. Here the Lord sits as a Mahayogi in the Harivarasanam posture, his knees bound by the yogapattam and his hand in chinmudra. In that mudra the index finger is the individual soul and the thumb is Brahman, and their touch shows the Upanishadic truth Tat Tvam Asi, “You are That.” Tradition calls Sabarimala a Mahayoga Peetham, and in the six-kshetra tradition it is the Ajna chakra, where the pilgrim’s journey reaches the third eye.

According to the Bhutanatha Upakhyanam, rishis and yogis meditating at Veliyanavattam built a golden temple for Manikantan. When his avatar was complete, he returned there and merged into its sacred seat. That subtle shrine is linked to Ponnambalamedu, where the Makara Jyothi appears.

Pilgrims go under a Guruswami. They keep a 42-day vratam, wear rudraksha or tulasi malas and black, saffron or blue clothes, and carry the Irumudi on their heads. It holds a coconut filled with ghee for the Lord’s abhishekam. At darshan, many devotees shed tears of joy, and most return year after year. At Sabarimala everyone is equal: the devotee and the deity share the same name, Ayyappa or Swami. Male pilgrims are called Ayyappans and female pilgrims Malikappurams. The shrine opens from mid-November to mid-January and for the first five days of every Malayalam month.

guides.title: The traditional path to Sabarimala (Periya Paatha)

intro.html:
Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa

Traditional Path

The Periya Paatha, also known as the long route or traditional path is said to be the path taken by Lord Ayyappa to kill Mahishi and also the path taken by King Rajashekhara to visit Sabarimala after the consecration of the holy shrine at Sabarimala.

Sabarimala Virtual Q: how to book your darshan slot

blocks.html:
Devotees undertake the Vrata (a vow or fast and discipline) for 42 days by wearing a Mala under the guidance of their Guru Swami, the Guru who will lead them on the pilgrimage. On the day of Kettu Nira (preparation of Irumudi), the Guruswami performs a Puja to invoke Lord Ayyappa and goes through the process of filling the ghee meant for the Abhisheka into a coconut. The ghee filled coconut, along with the other essential offerings for the Lord are then packed in a two compartment bag, referred to as the Irumudi. The Guruswami then places the sacred Irumudi on head of the pilgrims to the continuous chanting of Saranams. The pilgrim then leaves on the pilgrimage without bidding farewell to his family and friends.

Why ghee in a coconut?

The ghee filled into the coconut has a special significance in Ayyappa worship. The whole purpose of the Vratam is to condition the mind and body to undertake the pilgrimage to Sabarimala and offer the ghee to the Lord. The ghee we pour into the coconut is our atma (soul), and the coconut that holds it is our body: in essence, we are showing our complete surrender to the Supreme. With the Kettu Nira (Irumudi Puja), when the ghee is filled into the coconut, our atma is carried into the ghee-filled coconut.

On reaching Sabarimala and seeing Him, we offer Him the ghee as atma neivedhyam, and the coconut is given to the Agni. The atma attains liberation on being absorbed by the supreme soul: the jeevatma is the ghee and the paramatma is Lord Ayyappa. Once the ghee is removed, the coconut symbolizes jadam, the lifeless body. This is why the coconut is then offered into the huge Aazhi, the fire below the steps leading to the sanctum sanctorum.

Enga Guruswami Thunai Kondu Avar Paadham Nambikittu,
Irumudiya Sumandhukittu Vandhom Ayya

There are three routes to Sabarimala –

  1. The Erumeli route.
  2. The Vandiperiyar route.
  3. The Chalakayam route.

In the early days, Ayyappa devotees walked through the jungles from Erumeli to reach Sabari Malai. It is still believed that this route, covering approximately 50km, should be followed for a true Sabari Malai pilgrimage experience. This route is called ‘Peruvazhi paatha’, ‘Periyapathai’ or ‘The long route’. It is said that this route was the one used by Lord Ayyappa himself during his forest expedition to kill ‘Mahishi’ and that the King of Pandala ‘Pandalaraja’ took to visit Ayyappa’s shrine. Ayyappa devotees choose this route to experience the lord’s Poongaavanam (the Lord’s garden) to get closer to the Lord in mind, body, and spirit.

The nearest railway station to Erumeli is Kottayam or Chengannur. The nearest airports are at Kochi or Thiruvananthapuram. Devotees then take a bus or car to reach Erumeli. The chart below summarizes the Periyapathai yatra route from Erumeli to Sabarimala which goes through Perurthodu, Kottapadi, Irumpunnikara, Arasumudikota, Kaalaketti, Azhuthamedu, Kallidumkunnu, Inchipaarakotta, Mukkuzhi, Karivalanthodu, Karimala, Valiyaanavattam ,Cheriyaanavattam, Pamba River, Neelimala, Appachimedu, Sabaripeedam, and Saramkuthi. A brief description of each milestone during the Yatra follows.

blocks.alt: Map of the Sabarimala traditional trekking path, about 20.8 miles from Erumeli to Sabarimala

blocks.html: Petta thullal at Erumeli

The Erumeli Shastha temple

Erumeli Petta Thulli Vavaraya Vendikkitu Perur Thodil Pori Pottu Vandhom Ayya.

The name Erumeli is derived from “Erumakolli” (Killed the buffalo). According to legend, it was here that Lord Ayyappa killed the buffalo headed demoness “Mahishi”, sister of Mahishasura in this place on the way to collect leopard’s milk for his ailing mother. Mahish means buffalo and “Eruma” in Malayalam and hence the name “erumakolli”. This name later changed to Erumeli. The Dharma Shastha temple built by the king of Pandala is located here. Lord Dharma Shastha appears here as a hunter with a bow and arrow. There are two other small shrines adjacent to the main temple at Erumeli – one (mosque) dedicated to Vavar who was the trusted aide of the Lord and another – called Petta Shastha, in honor of Ayyappa himself.

Erumeli is synonymous with the famous Petta Thullal. It is said that after destroying Mahishi, Lord Ayyappa danced on her body. The ritual remembering this event is called Petta Thullal. The devotees paint colors on themselves with ashes, saffron and carbon and carry odd-looking arrows, clubs, bundles of fruits and vegetables. The essence of this practice is to give up ones’ ego and surrender to Lord Ayyappa. With Kanni Ayyappans lined up in the front, they dance rhythmically to the drum and cymbal beats and to the chants, ‘Ayyappa Thinthakathom, Swami Thinthakathom.’ Petta Thullal commences at the small Petta Shastha Ayyappa shrine and proceeds to the Dharma Shastha complex. It is obligatory for Kanni Ayyappans to participate in Petta Thullal. These rejoicings commemorate the joy of people after Mahishi was slain by Lord Ayyappa. Devotees then take a shower or bath and visit the Dharma Shastha temple to seek authorization from Lord Ayyappa to tread through the Poongaavanam (god’s garden) and the sacred hill Sabari.

Perur Thodu (meaning river) is the first landmark located about 3.2 km from Erumeli. This used to be a forest path, but has changed to a tar road path to accommodate commercial traffic. Lord Ayyappa rested here during his expedition. Devotees give alms here and put puffed rice into the river and continue the trek to the next major landmark – Kaalaketti. Enroute to Kaalaketti, there is a beautiful Shiva and Murugan shrine at Irumbunnikkara and also a temple for Goddess Bala Bhadra Devi. The forest beyond Perur Thodu is poongaavanam.

Kaalaketti Anjal Vandhu Azhutha Malai Erikittu Karimalaiyin Uchiyile Vandhom Ayya.

About 10 km from Perur Thodu is Kaalaketti. The legend says that Lord Shiva, Ayyappa’s father, came on his bull (‘Kaalai’) and tied (‘Ketti’) it here and witnessed Lord Ayyappa killing Mahishi. There is a shrine where the pilgrims light camphor and break coconuts. In the olden days, the path from Erumeli to Kaalaketti used to be a forest path. Due to commercialization (road side shops), the path has been made into a tar road.
Azhutha river
Kallidumkunnu

Injippara Vana Durga

Azhutha river, a tributary of Pamba, is about 2 kms from Kaalaketti. After a dip in Azhutha river, devotees take a small stone/pebble with them. On the far side of the river is the steep Azhuthamalai (hill), famous for its arduous track. After 2km of steep ascent, devotees reach Kallidumkunnu. The devotees drop the pebble taken by them from Azhutha River here. This is done as the mortal remains of Mahishi was cast off here and filled with stones. Injippaarakotta (Kotta means fort) is at the peak of Azhuthamalai where there is Kotayil Shastha shrine. Lord Ayyappa graces here in the name of Devan Vyakrapadan. Vyakram means Tiger. Lord is keeping the tigers under His control to protect His devotees. This also has a spiritual background. Men are occupied with material desires as gold, women and land and have little space in mind for sublime thoughts. Men are ready to do anything sinful to gain these desires. These desires are but brutal tigers. When such animal thoughts are shed off, the mind turns toward the Almighty.
Mukkuzhi Bhagavathi temple

Karivalanthodu

From Injippaarakotta the pilgrims descend the slippery path carefully. The devotees reach Mukkuzhi where Mother Ambika graces them. They then continue on for about 8kms of ups and downs to reach Karivalanthodu (canal) with Azuhtha hill on one side and Karimalai hill on the other. They will have to cross the river Puducherry here. There are some facilities for the devotees at Karivalanthodu where they can rest and relax before they ascend Karimala.

blocks.alt: The Kochu Kadutha Swami shrine at Karimala

blocks.html: Karimala is the abode of elephants which visits the Karimala canal to drink water. Pilgrims light the aazhi (campfire) to protect themselves from wild animals and cold weather. Karimala hill is very steep and consists of seven levels and is climbed in stages. As the ascent of 5 km is difficult the pilgrims continuously chant saranams. As there are powerful herbal plants with medicinal values here, it is said that after crossing the place, the devotee would be cured of any disease he is suffering from. On top of Karimala the terrain is flat suitable for the pilgrims to rest. Nearby are the Nazhikkinar – a well within a well with fresh spring like water, as well as deities of Karimalanathan, Kochukaduthaswami and Karimala Bhagavathi.
Periyaanavattam
Cheriyaanavattam

Pamba

Pambayile Kulichiputtu Pavangala Tholachuputtu Neelimalai Erikittu Vandhom Ayya.

From Karimala peak begins the 5km descent to Periyaanavattam. It is so named as there were huge numbers of elephants once. Pamba River flows here as a small stream. It is in its full form at a distance. After another 2.75km, devotees reach Cheriyaanavattam and the holy Pamba River. Devotees coming through Erumeli long route and those from the Chalakayam route meet on the banks of Pamba. It is as holy as Ganga. Lord Sri Rama performed Tarpan to His father Emperor Dasaratha in Pamba. Some devotees bathe in a place called Triveni Sangama – confluence of three rivers – and perform Tarpan to ancestors. Others bathe at the Pamba to wash themselves of their sins. Many devotees stay on the banks of Pamba for a night and light Pamba deepas (Pamba Vilakku). They then cook food from things they have brought in their Irumudi package. They offer it to Lord as Naivedhya and share with their pilgrim mates. It is believed that Lord Ayyappa accepts the food in the form of devotees. This is called Pamba Saddhi/ Saddhi Puja.
Appachimedu

Nadappandhal

Devotees begin climbing the Neelimalai after worshipping at the temple of Pamba Ganapathi, Sri Rama, Hanuman and Shakti temples. On the foot of the Neeli hill is the representative of the King of Pandalam. The pilgrims offer their respects to the representative. After seeking the permission of the representative to visit the shrine of Lord Ayyappa they proceed with their journey. From here the Sannidhanam is about 6 km. Neelimalai is as difficult as the Azhutha and Karimala. Knees would hit the ground while climbing. It is said that Sage Madhanga lived here with his daughter Neeli and performed penance to Lord Shiva, hence the name Neelimalai. A road branches from here called Subramaniya paatha. Things needed for pilgrims are transported through this path. Some people walk this path to reach or return from Sabari peedam. The top of Neeli hill is called Appachi medu. Here there are two abysses – Appachi Kuzhi and Ippachi Kuzhi. Kanniswami throw rice balls here to calm down the evil spirits present around the place and to please the jungle Gods- Vana Devathas.
Saramkuthi

Marakkoottam

Sabaripeedam is at the peak of Neelimalai. Lord Sri Rama’s celebrated devotee Sabari lived here after whom this name came into being. Devotees break coconuts here, show camphor Aarathi, worship and proceed further. The path is plain and comfortable for the devotees from here. The path toward the Ayyappa shrine bifurcates here. The left track is for transportation of goods and is also the return path. Devotees take the other track called Saramkuthi Paatha. For the Kanniswamis, Saramkuthi is considered very sacred. They place the wooden arrows they used during the Petta Thullal ritual in Erumeli in this place.

Pathinettam Padi Thaandi Bhagavane Unai Vendi Karpoora Jyothidanai Kandom Ayya.

The devotee feels the blissful experience on seeing the golden temple of Lord Ayyappa. The chanting sound “Saranam Ayyappa” echoes in all directions. In front of the sacred temple is the HOLY 18 steps (Pathinettampadi) all covered with gold. The 18 steps is made of black granite and was installed during the consecration of the temple. It has been covered with Panchaloha (five metals) to avoid wear and tear to the holy steps. Before placing their feet on the first step, the devotees worship Kaduthasami and Karuppusami, forgetting all the difficulties they experienced on the way to this great shrine. The devotees shed their ego by breaking the coconuts and begin climbing the steps with Saranams. As all the 18 steps represent a deity, only those with their Irumudi package are allowed to use the steps to reach the Sannidhanam. The Vedic reading ‘Tattvamasi’ greets the devotee at the entrance of the shrine. It is called from the Vedas, meaning ‘Thou art that. Devotees have to conquer, or climb over the 18 aspects that the 18 steps represent, to come to the realization that the GOD that they seek is already in them.

intro.html:
Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa

Observing the Vratam

The meaning of the Vratam is a “Vow” or “Resolution.” When you undertake the Vratam for your pilgrimage to Sabarimala, you are taking a vow to perform a certain set of activities, and a vow to not perform certain others.

This page explains the vratam and answers common questions from devotees, especially first-time pilgrims (Kanni Swamis). Customs vary between regions, temples and families, so treat this as general guidance. When in doubt, your Guruswami has the final word.

Last updated October 2026

blocks.html:
Deeksha (also called the vratam) is the sacred vow a devotee takes before going to Sabarimala. It begins the moment you wear the mala and continues until you return from the pilgrimage and remove it. Traditionally it lasts 42 days, which is one mandalam.

The purpose of the vratam is to cleanse the body and mind, and to prepare the devotee physically and mentally for the journey. In earlier days there was no short cut: devotees trekked the Peruvazhi (Periya Paatha, about 60 km) or the Pullumedu route, which was then longer and tougher than it is today, and walked all the way back after darshan. Today devotees can trek the Peruvazhi or the 7 km climb from Pamba to the Sannidhanam. Either way, you climb extremely steep mountains through large crowds.

The most important observances are celibacy and chanting Saranams. Each of the others also has a reason:

  • Bathe twice a day (morning and evening) in room temperature water, and avoid hot water. There is no hot water in the forest, so this conditions your body for the yatra.
  • Pray or meditate to Lord Ayyappa after each bath. This prepares you for the mental journey.
  • Eat only simple vegetarian (sattvic) food: no meat, fish or eggs, and no onion, garlic, drumstick or any food that is considered to be an aphrodisiac. See What can I eat during the vratam?
  • Do not drink alcohol or use tobacco. They weaken the body you are preparing for the trek, just as you would give them up when training for a marathon.
  • Practice strict celibacy (brahmacharya) in thought, words and actions.
  • Wear a black, blue, saffron or white dhoti. See What should I wear?
  • Do not shave, cut your hair or trim your nails.
  • Walk barefoot. You will walk barefoot over the rocks of the Lord’s Poongaavanam (forest).
  • Sleep on the floor or a mat without a pillow. There are no beds in the forest.
  • Be patient and speak gently in everything you do, from driving to talking with your family and coworkers, and avoid anger, gossip and arguments. A 60 km trek, not knowing what lies ahead, needs a lot of patience.
  • Address every other devotee as "Swami" (and women as "Malikappuram" or "Mataji"), because during the vratam every devotee is seen as a form of Ayyappa.

You do not need to leave home and stay in a secluded place during the vratam. That custom belongs to an earlier time; see What if women in the house have their monthly periods?

The aim is to purify the body and mind so that you climb the holy 18 steps (Pathinettam Padi) in the right spirit. The Deeksha ends after you return home, when the mala is removed with a small prayer, usually at a temple or in front of your Guruswami.

A Guruswami (also called Guru Swami) is a senior devotee who has completed the Sabarimala pilgrimage many times, traditionally at least 18 years, and who guides other devotees through the Deeksha and the yatra. He usually leads a group of devotees on the pilgrimage, and for a Kanni Swami (first-time pilgrim) his guidance is especially important.

The role of the Guruswami in Ayyappa worship:

  • Places the mala on the devotee with prayers, marking the start of the Deeksha.
  • Teaches the rules of the vratam and helps devotees keep them correctly, answering their doubts along the way.
  • Conducts the Kettunira (Irumudi Kettu) ceremony, where the Irumudi is filled and placed on the devotee’s head.
  • Leads the group on the pilgrimage, guiding the Saranam chanting and the customs at Erumeli, Pamba and the Sannidhanam.
  • Removes the mala at the end of the pilgrimage, completing the vratam.

Devotees treat their Guruswami with deep respect. By passing on what he has learned from his own Guru, he keeps the traditions of Sabarimala alive from one generation of Swamis to the next.

sections.title: What does the Mala Dharana mantra mean?

blocks.html:
When we wear the mudra mala, we are indeed making a physical, mental and spiritual commitment - with the Divine Self within, to prepare our body/mind/intellect for the arduous journey through the forests to reach His Divine abode, and to get His darshan. We commit to observing the vrata for at least one mandalam (of six weeks), go on the pilgrimage and present our Irumudi at HIS Holy Feet - for HIS divya darshan.

Given below are the shlokams we chant at the time of receiving our mudra mala from our guru, after having worshipped the Holy Feet of our Supreme Guru, Swami Ayyappa.

  1. JnAna mudrAm, shAstra mudrAm, guru mudrAm namAmyaham | vana mudrAm, shuddha mudrAm, rudra mudrAm namAmyaham ||
  2. ShAnta mudrAm, satya mudrAm, vrata mudrAm namAmyaham | shabaryAshrama satyena mudrAm pAtu sadApi me ||
  3. Guru -dakshiNayA poorvam tasyAnugraha kAriNe | sharaNAgata mudrAkhyam tvan mudrAm dhArayAmyaham ||
  4. Chin mudrAm, khechari mudrAm, bhadra mudrAm namAmyaham | shabaryAchala mudrAyai namas-tubhyam namo namaha ||

Let us explore the meaning and the significance of these four shlokams:

  1. My salutations to this symbol representing wisdom, the sacred scriptures, the Guru, the forest (representing life itself, through which we take the journey toward attaining moksha), purity and the ever-present God.
  2. I offer my salutations to this symbol of peace, truth, penance. May the Truth of Sabari's hermitage ever protect this symbol.
  3. After seeking and securing the compassionate grace and blessings of my Guru, O Lord, I will wear this symbol of my complete surrender, and seek refuge in You.
  4. I offer my salutation to this symbol of pure intellect, the celestial beings, and auspiciousness. O symbol of the sabari hill, I offer my salutations to you again and again.

There are a few important words and concepts to understand and appreciate in these shlokams. First, the word 'mudra'. Literally, mudra means a symbol, a seal (as in a royal seal, a seal of authority), a special sign (as mudras used in tantric rituals and our puja), and a special pose conveying specific meanings (e.g. classical dance has numerous mudras).

To devotees of Swami Ayyappa, the mudra mala is a seal of approval they have received from HIM, their Supreme Guru, through the compassionate grace and blessings of their guru swami. It is the honorable duty of the guru swami to ensure that the mudra mala is given only to the deserving. It is also the guru swami's duty to guide the devotee through out the vratam, and help through the journey to attain our Lord's darshanam. Thus, each mudra mala represents a symbol of the guru swami's authority, commitment and responsibility to the devotee.

The shlokams detail the many aspects/attributes which the mudra mala symbolizes, from wisdom all the way to total surrender of the self (ego) and finally seeking refuge at the Holy Feet of our Lord. It is equally important to appreciate that this surrender of self is not just at the feet of our Lord, but also at the feet of the guru swami.

It is also important to understand the expanded meaning of 'guru' or preceptor. It is said we have three preceptors who lead us to realization of the Divine Self within. The first of these is our mother, who bears us and nourishes us. The second is our father, who traditionally initiates us into Gayathri upaasana and leads us to the next preceptor - the one who imparts Vedic knowledge to us, preparing us for the Atma-vichaarana needed for realizing the Divine Self. Thus, it is essential to get the blessings of one's parents before approaching the guru swami for wearing a mudra mala and starting on the austerities leading to the yatra and the experience of bliss in His divine presence.

Which brings us to the next three key words: dakshina, anugraha and sharanaagati. The word dakshina has several meanings - but the most important of them is, "Compassionate, ignorance-destroying glance/communication". Our Lord is called Dakshinaamoorthi, as HIS compassionate glance and the chin-mudra HE shows completely dispels the nescience of the greatest of sages who had been in penance for thousands of years at HIS feet to attain knowledge of the Self.

The guru dakshina we offer to our guru is a very humble and a miniscule token offering in exchange for this divine compassion we receive. In fact, in order to be truly deserving of this grace, we need to do a lot more, there is a shlokam:

dhyAna moolam guror moortihi, pujA moolam guror padam mantra moolam guror vAkhyam, moksha moolam guror krupA

The foundation of meditation is the form of our guru; the foundation of worship are the holy feet of our guru. His words are the foundation of mantrams to us. (By being so) HIS grace becomes the foundation for liberation from earthly bondage. There is another shlokam that describes the dakshina to be given to a guru:

guru shushrUshayA vidya, pushkalena, dhanena cha athavA vidyayA vidyA, chaturthi nopalabhyate

In order to gain knowledge from a guru, you have to serve the guru (caring for the guru), and offer the guru all forms of wealth including money. Else, you should be able to impart to the guru some knowledge being sought by the guru (for example, I will teach you German, if you will teach me French). There is no fourth way (for gaining knowledge from a guru).

And Taittreeya Upanishad urges: 'AchAryAya priyam dhanam Ahrutya ...' give as much as needed to please the preceptor. It also states: shraddhayA deyam, a-shraddhayA a-deyam, shriyA deyam, hriyA deyam, bhiyA deyam, samvidA deyam - with reverence should offerings be given, never with irreverence, and given with liberality, modesty, fear and in friendliness.

So, with the dakshina of our guru secured, and through guru's 'anugraha' - which means, through the guru's decision to shower you with grace and blessings - you surrender your ego and seek refuge (sharaNAgati) at the Holy Feet of the Supreme Guru, our Lord Ayyappan. Note that this shlokam is directly addressing Lord Ayyappan - while the other three shlokams are focused on the mudra mala itself. The word literally means 'brought closely along' - the guru 'carries' you through the process from start to finish, till you are brought to the Divine presence of the Lord.

My prayers to Lord Ayyappan to bless us, his devotees with HIS mudra mala on the day of vrischika sankramaNam, be our constant inspiration and guide through the manDala vratam and our journey to HIS Divine sannidhAnam.

sections.title: I want to wear a mala for the first time. What should I do?

blocks.html:
Welcome, Kanni Swami! Here is the usual path:

  1. Find a Guruswami. This is an experienced devotee who has made the pilgrimage many times. He will guide you through the rules, help prepare your Irumudi, and usually leads your group to Sabarimala. If you don't have one, see I don't have a Guruswami or priest.
  2. Pick your start date. Count back 42 days from the day you plan to have darshan.
  3. Buy the mala and clothes. The mala is usually made of tulasi or rudraksha beads (108 or 54) with an Ayyappa locket. Also get two or three black, blue, saffron or white dhotis.
  4. Wear the mala. On the chosen day, take a bath, go to an Ayyappa temple (or any temple), and have your Guruswami or the temple priest place the mala around your neck while you recite the Mala Dharana mantra. Some families do this at home in front of the puja room, with parents giving the mala.
  5. Begin the Deeksha rules from that moment.
  6. Join group bhajans and pujas during the 42 days, and attend as many as possible. They are a big part of the experience.
  7. Prepare the Irumudi with your Guruswami before you leave for Sabarimala. Kanni Swamis traditionally have a few extra customs (such as the Kanni puja), and your Guruswami will explain these.

sections.title: I don't have a Guruswami or priest. Who can help me wear the mala for the first time?

blocks.html:
This is common, and it shouldn't stop you from taking the vratam. Devotees in your position usually do one of the following:

  • Go to a temple. Any Ayyappa temple will have a priest who places malas for devotees during the season, often on the first day of Vrishchikam. You don't need to know him beforehand; you can just walk in. If there's no Ayyappa temple nearby, a priest at any Hindu temple (Ganesha, Shiva, Murugan or Vishnu) can do it.
  • Have a parent or elder do it. In many families, the mother or father places the mala around the devotee's neck in front of the home puja room. This is considered just as sacred.
  • Wear it yourself before Ayyappa. Take a bath, light a lamp in front of a picture of Lord Ayyappa, place the mala at his feet, pray, and then wear it yourself while reciting the Mala Dharana mantra or simply chanting "Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa." Tradition holds that Ayyappa himself is the ultimate Guru, so devotees in this situation accept him as their Guru.

Even if you wear the mala on your own, try to join a local Ayyappa bhajan group or a group traveling to Sabarimala during your 42 days. An experienced Swami is important for the practical parts: preparing your Irumudi (kettu nira), Kanni Swami customs, and guiding you on the trek. Ayyappa temples and Ayyappa seva sanghams can usually connect you with a group. If you live outside India, ask at your local Hindu temple.

sections.title: When can I start wearing the mala?

blocks.html:
Most devotees wear the mala on the first day of the Malayalam month of Vrishchikam, which falls in mid-November. This lines up the 42 days with the Mandala Puja in late December.

You don't have to start on that exact day, though. The general rule is to start 42 days before the day you plan to visit Sabarimala. For example, if your group plans to go for Makaravilakku in mid-January, you would start around the first week of December. Choose an auspicious day suggested by your Guruswami and confirm the date with him.

sections.title: Can I start Deeksha without wearing the mala?

blocks.html:
Yes. You can begin the observances of the vratam, such as vegetarian food, celibacy, bathing twice a day in room temperature water (avoiding hot water to condition our body in preparation for the Yatra) and daily prayer, before the mala is placed on you. Some devotees do this for a few days to prepare themselves, or when constraints such as travel keep them from reaching their Guruswami or a temple right away.

Talk to your Guruswami to plan your start date (count back 42 days from the day of your yatra) and fix a day with him to wear the mala.

sections.title: Can I wear the mala for just 1 or 2 weeks?

blocks.html:
The traditional and recommended period is 42 days, and many Guruswamis insist on it, especially for a Kanni Swami going to climb the 18 steps with an Irumudi.

You can also observe Deeksha for more than 42 days if you wish. Some devotees go to Sabarimala several times a year and stay in an extended period of vratam across those visits.

Anything shorter than 42 days is not the full vratam. If your work or family situation makes the full 42 days difficult, discuss your constraints with your Guruswami; do not decide on your own.

If a full vratam is not possible this year, you can also visit Sabarimala for darshan without the mala and Irumudi. You simply cannot climb the holy 18 steps; you use the alternate path instead.

sections.title: What should I wear, and what do the colors mean?

blocks.html:
During the vratam, devotees set aside their everyday clothes and wear a simple dhoti (mundu, veshti or panchakacham) in black, blue, saffron or white, with a shirt or a towel (angavastram) over the shoulder. The color applies only to the dhoti, not to your entire outfit. Each color has its own significance:

Black

Black stands for giving up worldly pleasures and ego. It is also the color of Lord Saneeshwara, who is ebony black. Swamis who suffer from Sani Dosham are instructed by their Guruswamis to wear black so that they may be released from Sani’s harsh influence. They are also guided to chant the 12 stotras that please Saneeshwara as they climb Sabarimala, so that by the time they reach the top, Sani Bhagavan has removed himself from their lives.

Blue

The Lord is described as Neela Megha Shyamala Varnan, dark as a rain cloud. Devotees wear blue, usually dark blue, to associate themselves with the Lord.

Saffron (Kavi)

Saffron is the color of sannyasa (renunciation). Devotees who live the life of a sanyasi within the grihasthashrama, with detached attachment, wear kavi to show that they are living like an ascetic for the period of the vow. It is often preferred by senior devotees.

White

Devotees who devote their attention entirely to Him, without any self-interest, wear white veshtis, as they consider Him as Nirguna Bhagavan. In Keralam, most Swamis still wear white, and some deekshadharis wear a panchakacham through the entire Deeksha period.

Whatever the color, the clothes make every devotee look alike, rich or poor, so that all stand equal before Ayyappa as “Swami”. They also remind the devotee, and everyone around him, that he is under a sacred vow.

For office or work, many Swamis keep their clothes simple, clean and modest, and change into traditional dress at home and at the temple. For shoes at work, see Can I wear shoes or chappals?

sections.title: Can I wear shoes or chappals, for example at work?

blocks.html:
Traditionally, devotees walk barefoot for the entire 42 days as an act of humility and discipline.

Practically, many working Swamis need footwear, for example for safety reasons at factories, construction sites, labs, hospitals, or because of a long commute. Common approaches are:

  • Go barefoot at home, at the temple, and wherever else you reasonably can.
  • If your workplace requires safety shoes, wear them. Safety comes first, and most Guruswamis accept this.
  • Remove footwear as soon as you no longer need it, and wash your feet before prayers.
  • Avoid leather accessories including footwear, belt, etc. if possible.
  • Tell your Guruswami about your work situation when you take the mala so he can guide you.

sections.title: Can I shave or cut my hair after I wear the mala?

blocks.html:
No. During Deeksha, devotees do not shave, cut their hair or trim their nails. This is a sign of giving up attention to physical appearance during the vratam. You can resume after the pilgrimage, when the mala is removed.

This applies at work too. Many Swamis tell their colleagues that they are observing the vratam and grow a beard for its duration.

sections.title: What can I eat during the vratam?

blocks.html:
Eat only simple vegetarian (sattvic) food:

  • No meat, fish or eggs.
  • No onion, garlic, drumstick or any food that is considered to be an aphrodisiac.
  • No alcohol or tobacco.

Pray to the Lord before each meal and thank Him for it. Lord Ayyappa is Annadhaana Prabhu, so try to feed the poor whenever possible. If you live in the US, consider making prasadam, taking it to the temple and sharing it with other devotees.

Avoid processed or packaged food; it only hurts your body, which you are trying to bring to as perfect a state as possible for the pilgrimage. If practical, eat only food cooked fresh at home by a person who has bathed and prayed before cooking. Food from the previous day is considered stale and should not be eaten. Eat fresh fruit instead of chips and other junk food.

Many Swamis also eat lightly to prepare for the little food available on the trek: replace one meal a day (breakfast or dinner) with fruit, eat rice only once a day, and round out meals with chapati or similar.

Don’t eat at restaurants unless you are traveling. Restaurant kitchens handle meat and vegetarian food together.

sections.title: Can my family eat non-vegetarian food or eggs while I am wearing the mala?

blocks.html: Traditionally, the whole household follows a vegetarian diet while a Swami is observing Deeksha, and eggs count as non-vegetarian. Many families also avoid alcohol and smoking at home during this period, because the Swami's surroundings are expected to stay pure.

sections.title: I am a bachelor living with others who cook and eat non-vegetarian food. How do I manage?

blocks.html:
This is common for students and young professionals, and you can still observe the vratam well with a little planning:

  • Talk to your roommates. Explain the vratam and how long it lasts. Most people are happy to help once they understand.
  • Keep your own cookware. Use separate pots, pans, plates and utensils, and store your food separately.
  • Cook at a different time. Agree on a time when you have the kitchen to yourself, and clean the stove and counter before you start.
  • Keep a clean space for prayer. Set aside a corner of your room for a lamp and a picture of Ayyappa.
  • Eat with fellow Swamis when you can. Many temples serve annadanam during the Mandalam season, and group bhajans and pujas usually end with prasadam.
  • Avoid eating out. Restaurant kitchens handle meat and vegetarian food together. Simple, fresh meals you cook yourself are better.

What matters most is your own discipline. Do your best with the space you have, and ask your Guruswami if you need guidance.

sections.title: How do I follow the vratam in the US?

blocks.html:
Yes, you can observe the vratam fully while living in the US, with a few practical adjustments.

The core principle

A senior Guruswami who has been going to Sabarimala for over half a century holds one principle above all: Lord Ayyappa is our bosom friend. Surrender completely to Him (sharanagati) and keep Brahmacharya; follow everything else in the spirit of the vow.

Every day

  • Bathe twice a day in room temperature water, avoiding hot water, and pray or meditate after each bath.
  • Recite the Namaskara Shlokam (Loka Veeram) and chant as many Saranams as you can. Each Saranam tells Lord Ayyappa that you surrender to Him.
  • Pray before each meal and thank Ayyappa, the Annadhana Prabhu, for your food.
  • Practice patience in everything, from driving to talking with family and coworkers. The trek to Sabarimala will test it.

At work

  • It is fine to wear shoes at work; take them off whenever you can. See Can I wear shoes or chappals?
  • Do not shave or cut your hair. Many devotees tell their colleagues about the vratam and grow a beard.
  • Keep your mind on God and on your work, and stay calm and patient with everyone.

At home and on weekends

  • Wear a black, blue, saffron or white dhoti.
  • Walk barefoot, and sleep on the floor or a mat without a pillow.
  • Avoid parties, and visits to the homes of people who are not observing the vratam.

Food

  • Follow the food rules in What can I eat during the vratam? No onion, garlic, drumstick or any food that is considered to be an aphrodisiac.
  • Don’t eat at restaurants unless you are traveling.

Temple and community

  • Visit temples as many times as possible during the Deeksha period.
  • Attend Ayyappa pujas and join Ayyappa bhajans in your area. Lord Ayyappa loves songs and bhajans, as the many devotional albums released in His praise each year show.
  • Look for opportunities to help organize pujas and assist fellow devotees. At Sabarimala all are equal: the Swami trekking beside you could be a company CEO or a laborer, and you would never know.

Above all, keep your mind pure and your thoughts on Ayyappa. Your Guruswami can guide you on anything specific to your situation.

sections.title: I live outside India. Can I wear the mala and do the Irumudi without going to Sabarimala?

blocks.html:
Yes. Many devotees outside India do this, and it is a widely accepted practice. Still, nothing can replace going to Sabarimala and climbing the holy 18 steps.

Wearing the mala and observing the vratam is no problem anywhere in the world. The 42-day Deeksha is a personal discipline, and many Ayyappa devotees abroad observe it fully while living and working overseas.

Irumudi without going to Sabarimala is where practice varies. Traditionally, the Irumudi is made for the Sabarimala pilgrimage: you carry it on your head up the holy 18 steps, and the ghee-filled coconut is offered to Ayyappa there. Outside India, many Hindu temples with an Ayyappa shrine hold an Irumudi ceremony during the Mandalam season, often around Mandala Puja or Makaravilakku. Devotees prepare the Irumudi (kettu nira) with the temple priest and carry it into the temple (some temples set up symbolic 18 steps for this). The ghee is offered for abhishekam to the Ayyappa vigraha, and the mala is then removed at the temple, completing the vratam.

How it is viewed:

  • Many priests and Guruswamis see this as a sincere and valid way to complete your vow when travel to India isn't possible. The devotion and discipline of the 42 days are what matter most.
  • Some traditionalists believe the full Irumudi pilgrimage can only be completed at Sabarimala. Devotees who share this view observe the vratam locally and complete it with a temple offering without an Irumudi, saving the Irumudi for when they can travel to Sabarimala.

What to do next:

  • Contact Hindu temples near you and ask whether they hold a Mandala Puja or Irumudi ceremony and whether they have an Ayyappa shrine. Many temples outside India do, and they usually announce dates around October or November.
  • Ask the priest how they guide first-time devotees. They can help you wear the mala, prepare the Irumudi, and remove the mala at the end.
  • Ask about local Ayyappa devotees or bhajan groups. They often organize these ceremonies together.

sections.title: I need to travel abroad on business. How do I manage airport security and food in other countries?

blocks.html:
Many Swamis travel for work during the Mandalam season, and the vratam can continue on the road with a little preparation.

At the airport

  • A tulasi or rudraksha mala rarely sets off security scanners, so you can usually keep it on. If an officer asks to check it, explain calmly that it is a religious item. If you must take it off, hold it in your hand or keep it in a clean pouch, and put it back on with a Saranam straight after.
  • Wearing shoes while traveling is fine. Take them off whenever you can, such as in your hotel room.
  • Keep up your morning and evening prayers. Many airports have a quiet multi-faith prayer room, and a small picture of Ayyappa fits in any bag.

On the flight

  • Pre-order a vegetarian meal when you book. Choose Asian Vegetarian (AVML) or Jain Meal or Vegan (VGML). Avoid the “Hindu meal” (HNML), which usually contains meat.
  • Carry dry snacks such as nuts, roasted chana or khakhra. Finish any fresh fruit before landing, as many countries do not allow it through customs.

At your destination

  • Look for “pure veg” Indian or South Indian restaurants, which keep meat out of the kitchen.
  • Book a hotel room with a kettle or kitchenette, and pack quick foods such as instant upma, poha or oats.
  • Visit a local Hindu or Ayyappa temple if there is one. Many serve prasadam or simple meals.
  • At business dinners, politely decline meat, eggs and alcohol and mention that you are observing a religious vow. Colleagues almost always respect this.

If a long trip falls close to your yatra, talk to your Guruswami beforehand about planning your Deeksha around it.

sections.title: What if Amavasya or a Shraddham (ancestral ritual) falls during my Deeksha?

blocks.html: There are no restrictions on performing Tharpanam or Shraddham for your ancestors during Deeksha. In fact, performing these rituals during Deeksha is a must. Devotees also perform these rituals during the Yatra at Pamba, Azhutha or other river banks before climbing Neelimala.

sections.title: What if women in the house have their monthly periods during my Deeksha?

blocks.html:
In many traditional homes, the Swami keeps some distance from women in the household during their periods, as part of the purity rules of the vratam. How strictly this is followed varies a lot between families and regions. Common practical arrangements include:

  • The Swami or another family member looks after the puja room and lamp during those days.
  • The Swami prepares his own food, or another family member cooks for him.
  • Separate sleeping arrangements, which are simple since the Swami already sleeps on the floor or a mat.
  • Keeping separate plates and utensils for the Swami, if your family follows this custom.

In the past, devotees in Keralam often stayed in the temple mandapam during the Mandalam season, because homes did not have room for this separation. That is no longer expected; you do not need to leave home.

Above all, handle this with care and respect. The women in your family are supporting your vratam, so plan the arrangements together in advance, and ask your Guruswami how your tradition handles it.

sections.title: There is a birth in the family. What do I do?

blocks.html:
Congratulations on the new arrival. A birth brings a shorter period of ritual impurity (sutakam, called vallayma in Keralam) for close relatives, usually about 10 days. Unlike a death, a birth is an auspicious event, so it does not normally require you to give up the vratam.

  • Before you wear the mala. Wait until the sutakam period is over and the house has been purified, then choose your start date with your Guruswami.
  • While you are wearing the mala. Most Guruswamis say you may keep the mala on. Keep up your daily prayers and observances, and take part in the family’s joy with care. If you are a close relative (such as the father or a grandparent), it is customary to avoid cooking for the household, to avoid ceremonies and temple rituals in the house until the purification is done, and to follow your Guruswami’s advice on visiting the mother and baby.
  • Before your yatra. If the birth falls close to your departure, finish the sutakam period (and the purification ritual, if your family follows one) before you leave for Sabarimala. If the dates clash, ask your Guruswami whether to delay the trip.
  • A distant relative or friend. Continue the vratam as usual. Visiting after your bath and prayers is generally fine.

sections.title: There is a death in the family. What do I do?

blocks.html:
We are sorry for your loss. A death in the family brings a period of ritual impurity (pula) for close relatives, usually observed for 10 to 16 days depending on the community. Traditionally, this affects the vratam as follows:

  • Before you wear the mala. Wait until the pula period and the final rites are complete. Your Guruswami can help you choose a new start date.
  • While you are wearing the mala. If a close family member passes away, the usual practice is to remove the mala, with your Guruswami’s guidance, so you can take part in the funeral and rites. After the pula period you can begin the vratam again if there is still time before your yatra, or plan for the next season.
  • A distant relative or friend. Many devotees continue the vratam but do not attend the funeral or visit the house of mourning while wearing the mala.
  • Loss of a parent or spouse. Some families do not undertake the pilgrimage until the first year of mourning is over.

Customs vary widely here, so speak to your Guruswami as soon as you can. Above all, take care of your family at this time; Ayyappa understands.

sections.title: A woman in my family wants to wear the mala. Can she?

blocks.html:
Yes, women can wear the mala, but what is traditionally followed depends mainly on her age. Female devotees are called Malikappuram (or "Mataji" in some regions).

If she is under 10 or over 50: She can wear the mala and do the full vratam and pilgrimage, including the Irumudi and climbing the holy 18 steps. Many young girls and older women go to Sabarimala every season. The vratam rules are the same as for men: vegetarian food, prayers twice a day, black, blue, saffron or white clothes and simple living.

If she is between about 10 and 50: By long-standing tradition, women of this age group do not go to Sabarimala or take the mala for the pilgrimage. The tradition is linked to Lord Ayyappa's form at Sabarimala as a Naishtika Brahmachari (eternal celibate). Women in this age group often take part in the season in other ways:

  • Observing the vratam disciplines at home (vegetarian food, daily prayers, bhajans) alongside the family Swamis, without wearing the mala.
  • Helping with Irumudi preparation and pujas at home.
  • Worshipping at local Ayyappa or other temples during the Mandalam season.

Outside India, some temples allow women devotees to take part in Mandala Puja ceremonies at their local Ayyappa shrine. Practices vary a lot, so it is best to ask the temple priest directly.

Whatever her age, speak with your Guruswami or temple priest about how they guide women devotees.

intro.html:
Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa

Sabarimala Virtual Q Explained

Every pilgrim to the Sabarimala Sannidhanam needs a Virtual Q slot. This guide explains what the Virtual Q is, the documents to keep ready, how to create your profile and book your slot, and what happens if you don't get one.

sections.title: What is the Sabarimala Virtual Q?

blocks.html:
The Sabarimala Virtual Q is an online reservation and crowd-management system run by the Kerala Police and the Travancore Devaswom Board (TDB) for pilgrims visiting the Sabarimala Sannidhanam temple in Keralam, India.

Key details of the system

  • Purpose: It regulates the flow of devotees, prevents massive overcrowding at Pamba and the Sannidhanam, and ensures a safer, more orderly darshan of Lord Ayyappa.
  • Free booking: The virtual queue slot booking is completely free of cost.
  • Daily caps: The system limits online slots (typically around 70,000 slots per day, with limited spot-booking alternatives available at designated centers). This number changes from year to year, and sometimes mid-season, depending on the rush.
  • Registration process: Pilgrims must register on the official portal using a valid mobile number or email address, upload required identity details/photos, and select a preferred date, time slot, and route.
  • Exemptions: Children under the age of 5 are exempt from the virtual queue requirement.
  • Verification: Upon booking, devotees receive a virtual queue coupon or QR code that must be verified along with original photo ID cards at designated police/board counters (such as at Pamba).

Book your slot and check for official updates on the Travancore Devaswom Board's official website: sabarimalaonline.org

To book a Virtual Q slot, you first create an official pilgrim profile and then reserve your time slot. Make sure you have the following digital files saved on your computer or mobile device before opening the website:

  • Photograph: A clear, passport-size digital photo of each pilgrim (the allowed file size ranges from 30 KB to 1 MB depending on the upload field, so compress the photo for a smooth upload).
  • Identity proof: A government-issued photo ID (such as an Aadhaar Card, Voter ID, or Passport). School or college ID cards are acceptable for children between 5 and 18 years old.
  • Active contact info: A working mobile number and email address to receive One-Time Passwords (OTPs).

sections.title: How to create your profile (sign up)

blocks.html:
1. Go to the official Sabarimala online portal.
  2. Click the "Register" or "Sign Up" button on that portal's homepage (not the Sign Up button on this website).
  3. Fill in your personal details, including your Name, Address, Date of Birth, and Gender.
  4. Choose your ID proof type (e.g., Aadhaar) and enter the exact Identity Card Number.
  5. Upload your passport photo from your device.
  6. Create a secure password, agree to the terms and conditions, and click "Continue".
  7. Enter the OTP sent via SMS to your mobile number to verify and activate your profile account.

sections.title: How to book your Virtual Q slot

blocks.html:
1. Log in: Use your newly registered mobile number or email address along with your password to access the portal.
  2. Navigate to booking: Click on the "Virtual Q Booking" icon on your main user dashboard.
  3. Add group members (optional): If you are traveling with a group, click "Add Pilgrim" or "Create Group" to add up to 5 co-pilgrims by typing in their individual details, IDs, and uploading their photos. Note: Children under 5 do not require a slot.
  4. Check availability: View the calendar.
    • Green dates have available slots.
    • Red dates are completely booked/sold out.
  5. Select details: Click on a green date, then choose your preferred Time Slot (hourly block) and Trekking Route (e.g., the standard Pamba-Sannidhanam path).
  6. Confirm and download: Click "Book Now" to confirm. Your Virtual Q Coupon, with a unique QR code, your photo and your slot time, will be generated. Download the PDF to your phone and print a copy to carry with you.
  7. Carry the printed coupon and the original ID you used for the booking when you go to Sabarimala. Photocopies of the ID are not accepted.

sections.title: What happens if I don't get a Virtual Q slot?

blocks.html:
If you travel to Sabarimala without a pre-booked Virtual Q ticket, you will still be allowed to have a darshan of Lord Ayyappa, but you will face significant administrative hurdles, very long wait times, and the risk of being turned away if crowd limits are reached.

The government and the Kerala High Court have put strict rules in place to manage the heavy rush, but there is one fallback for pilgrims who arrive without an online booking:

Spot booking counters

The Travancore Devaswom Board (TDB) operates official Spot Booking Centers at key transit hubs leading to the temple (such as Nilakkal and Vandiperiyar).

  • The process: You must physically queue up at these counters, present a valid government-issued photo ID (like your Aadhaar Card, Passport, or Voter ID), and have your information digitized.
  • The catch: These spot-booking slots are strictly capped and allocated dynamically based on cancellations. If the daily quota is already exhausted by the time you reach the counter, you will not receive a pass and could face major delays.

The risks of skipping the Virtual Q

If you choose to bypass the online system entirely, be prepared for the following consequences:

  • Extreme waiting times: Online Virtual Q ticket holders are funneled into a separate, faster-moving queue at the Pathinettampadi (18 Holy Steps). Non-ticket holders or those waiting for open slots face unpredictable, massive bottlenecks that can add many hours to the trek.
  • Sudden quota reductions: During peak season rush (like the Mandalam-Makaravilakku festival), the Kerala High Court frequently orders the TDB to drastically cut down or completely suspend spot bookings at standard locations like Pamba or Erumeli to prevent stampedes. If you rely on spot booking during these times, you risk not being allowed past the transit camps.
  • Disrupted travel plans: The Kerala Police strictly enforce time slots. Arriving without a confirmed time means you may be forced to wait at the base camps (Nilakkal or Pamba) until a dynamic slot frees up, throwing off your entire travel, food, and lodging schedule.

intro.html:
Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa

House Puja and Bhajan

How to host an Ayyappa Puja and Bhajan at your residence: preparing your home, the puja items, sattvik prasadam, the order of the evening, and what to do after.

blocks.html:
What is a house bhajan?

A house bhajan is an Ayyappa Puja and Bhajan held at a devotee's residence. Families and friends gather to sing bhajans, perform the puja, and conclude with Padi Paatu (the song of the 18 holy steps) and aarti.

What should be the main focus of the evening?

Devotion and the puja itself. The bhajan is a time to come together in prayer, not a social dinner. Please keep the emphasis on the singing, the rituals and Lord Ayyappa, rather than on food or elaborate arrangements.

Do I need to be an expert to host?

No. A sincere heart matters far more than perfection. Volunteers from the samaaj will guide the puja; the host's role is to prepare the space and the items listed below.

Do we need a priest?

Not necessarily. Samaaj volunteers can guide the puja. If you would like to invite one, look at it as an opportunity to encourage and support local priests or your family's house priest.

When should I have everything ready?

Please prepare all puja items in advance on the day of the event, before devotees arrive. Last-minute shopping takes attention away from the puja.

How should I set up the puja space?

Choose a clean, quiet area with enough room for devotees to sit on the floor. Place the Ayyappa picture or idol on a raised, clean surface, with space in front for the Ganesha, lamps, and the padi (steps) arrangement.

What if I don't have a photo of Ayyappa?

Contact the Ayyappa Samaaj volunteers. They will give you a high-resolution image that you can print and mount in a frame.

How many people should I plan for?

Check with the samaaj coordinator for the expected number. Keep seating simple: floor mats or sheets work well.

Whom should I invite?

The invitation should be open to all deekshadharis. Beyond them, please invite people who are devoted and will take part in the puja and bhajans. A house bhajan is a prayer gathering, not a party, and the evening goes best when everyone joins in.

Do I need to decorate elaborately?

No. Fresh flowers and well-lit lamps are enough. Simplicity keeps the focus on devotion.

What items do I need to prepare?

Please have the following ready in advance. Tick each off as you gather it.

checklist.text: Flowers: a garland plus 3–4 bouquets of loose flowers
2 lamps to place near the idols (silver or bronze)
2 small lamps for deepa aradhana and padi vilakku (silver or bronze)
18 or 36 agal clay lamps, or LED tea-light lamps
Oil and wicks for lamps, plus a matchbox or lighter
Fruits: bananas are a must; apples and others
Camphor and a plate to light it (1 full packet)
2 large plates (thambalam) to hold the aarti

blocks.html:
Why do we light the 18 step lamps?

Each of the 18 holy steps (padi) to Lord Ayyappa's sannidhanam is a deity. We sing Padi Paatu and light a lamp for each step to pay our respects to the sacred 18 steps and the deities of the 18 steps. Use one lamp per step, or two per step for 36.

What if I don't have an 18-step structure?

Ask the Ayyappa Samaaj or one of the devotees. They will lend you their steps.

Can I use LED tea lights instead of clay lamps?

Yes. LED tea lights are a safe, acceptable alternative, especially in homes with children or sensitive smoke alarms.

Why so much camphor?

The camphor flame should keep burning throughout Padi Paatu, so keep a full packet at hand.

What kind of prasadam should I prepare?

Sattvik prasadam only. Please do not use onion or garlic in anything offered or served. Simple, pure vegetarian preparations are ideal.

How elaborate should the prasadam be?

Keep it simple. The focus of the bhajan is devotion and the puja, not the prasadam items. One or two modest offerings are perfectly appropriate; a large spread is not expected.

What are good sattvik options?

  • Paanagam (already on the puja list)
  • Fresh fruits, especially bananas
  • Sweet pongal or payasam
  • Sundal (chickpea or other lentils)
  • Curd rice or lemon rice, if serving a light meal

How do I make paanagam?

This makes about 10 small servings.



Ingredients

  • 4 cups water
  • 1 cup grated jaggery
  • ½ tsp dry ginger powder (sukku)
  • ¼ tsp cardamom powder
  • Juice of 1 lemon

Method

  1. Dissolve the jaggery in the water, stirring well.
  2. Strain it through a fine sieve or cloth to remove any grit.
  3. Stir in the dry ginger and cardamom.
  4. Add the lemon juice and mix. Taste and adjust the jaggery or lemon.
  5. Make it fresh on the day and offer it at room temperature.

What should I avoid?

Onion, garlic, non-vegetarian items, eggs and alcohol. Avoid stale or leftover food; prasadam should be freshly prepared.

Can other devotees bring prasadam?

Yes, if coordinated with the host. The same sattvik, no onion/garlic guideline applies to everything brought.

What is the usual order of the evening?

Either of these two formats can be followed. Format 1 does the sahasranamam and ashtottaram before the bhajans; Format 2 starts with the bhajans and does the ashtottaram after the Ayyappa bhajans.



Format 1: Archana first

  1. Ganesha puja
  2. Light lamps around the deities
  3. Maha sankalpam
  4. Sahasranamam
  5. Ashtottaram
  6. Dhoopam
  7. Deepam
  8. Paanagam neivedyam
  9. Deeparadhana
  10. All other deity bhajans
  11. Deeparadhana when starting Ayyappa bhajans
  12. Ayyappa bhajans
  13. Dhoopam
  14. Deepam
  15. Maha neivedyam
  16. Padi Paatu with lighting of padi vilakku
  17. Mantra pushpam
  18. Namaskara shlokam
  19. Maha mangala aarathi
  20. Prasadam distribution

Format 2: Bhajans first

  1. Ganesha puja
  2. Light lamps around the deities
  3. Maha sankalpam
  4. All other deity bhajans
  5. Deeparadhana when starting Ayyappa bhajans
  6. Ayyappa bhajans
  7. Ashtottaram
  8. Dhoopam
  9. Deepam
  10. Paanagam neivedyam
  11. Maha neivedyam
  12. Padi Paatu with lighting of padi vilakku
  13. Mantra pushpam
  14. Namaskara shlokam
  15. Maha mangala aarathi
  16. Prasadam distribution

Should we do an ashtottaram or a sahasranamam?

Either can be included. An ashtottaram (108 names) takes about 5 minutes; a sahasranamam (1,000 names) takes about 30 minutes. Choose based on the time you have.

Should we include our family deity?

Yes. It is customary to also do the ashtottaram of your kula deivam (family deity).

What should devotees wear?

Traditional or modest clothing is encouraged. Many devotees wear black, blue or saffron in keeping with Ayyappa tradition.

Any etiquette to keep in mind?

  • Arrive on time and remove footwear before entering.
  • Silence or set phones aside during the puja.
  • Join in the singing; no prior experience is needed.
  • Keep conversation for after the aarti.

Any safety tips?

Keep lamps and camphor away from curtains and children, have water nearby, and consider temporarily covering nearby smoke detectors only if safe and permitted.

Can I perform abhishekam at home?

Abhishekam is recommended only in temples. If you do perform it at home, use a vigraha that is 3 inches or less in size, preferably one you already have at home. Doing abhishekam with a vigraha brought from the temple is not recommended. If you wish to have an abhishekam done, please consider sponsoring one at the temple.

Do's and Don'ts



✔ Do

  • Take a shower before the puja and wear clean clothes.
  • Keep the focus on devotion, the bhajans and the puja.
  • Keep all prasadam sattvik, with no onion or garlic.
  • For an evening puja, prefer simple palagaram: idly or pongal with chutney and sambar, curd rice, and chakkarapongal.

✘ Don't

  • Don't spend too much time on decorations.
  • Don't treat it as a competition. It is not one.
  • Don't make a large number of items. A few simple dishes are enough.

Should I clear the puja station after the bhajan?

No. Please leave the puja station as it is after the bhajan.

What do I do the day after?

  1. Perform an ashtottaram (108 names) for the deity.
  2. Offer a fresh prasadam (sattvik, no onion or garlic).
  3. Do deeparadhana.
  4. Only then remove all the puja items.

What do I do with the items once removed?

Flowers and leftover offerings can be respectfully placed in a garden or plant soil. The turmeric Ganesha can be dissolved in water and poured into a plant. Coconuts and fruits are shared as prasadam.

What if I can't find a specific item?

Contact the samaaj coordinator before the event. Most items can be substituted or borrowed, so please don't let one missing item stop you from hosting.
